title: The Veda kept by heart
hookLine: a student told to give back everything he learned, partridges who pick it up, and how the Veda has been kept by ear, join by join
carry: shruti: the Veda is heard, and kept by heart
tomorrow: a king beaten by a sage wants a new name. which one?
last: THE WIDE HEART COUNTS THE WHOLE EARTH AS FAMILY.

cards: As the Vishnu Purana tells it, the sage Vaishampayana teaches the Yajur Veda to his students. One day he needs a penance done for a fault, and his brightest student, Yajnavalkya, says: why ask these weaklings?
I'll do it alone. The teacher is furious. Then give back everything I taught you.
And Yajnavalkya does. He brings the Veda back up out of his body, every verse. The other students turn into partridges, tittiri, and peck it up.
That's the story behind the Taittiriya, the partridges' branch of the Yajur Veda. And Yajnavalkya, with nothing left, turns to the Sun, and the Sun teaches him the Veda anew.

teach.b: Notice what the Veda is in that story: not a book. Something learned by ear and carried inside a person. That's the Hindu teaching of shruti, what is heard.
The Vedas are held to be heard by the ancient seers, not composed, and passed from teacher's mouth to student's ear. To keep every syllable exact, reciters learned each hymn two ways.
The samhita, the putting together, with every join made.
And the padapatha, word by word, with every join undone.

Then they went further, chanting the words in patterns, in pairs, forward and back, so a single slip would be heard. In 2003, UNESCO recognized this Vedic chanting as a treasure of humanity's heritage.
Our week's joins work the same way. Namaste comes apart into a bow, to you, and the bow is to the divine in the other. Tat tvam asi splits into one, or two.
Karmany eva gives back karmani: in action alone, offered to Krishna. Jagannath gives back the world he's lord of.

teach.h: THE VEDA IS HEARD, AND KEPT BY HEART.
teach.b: Vasudhaiva lets go of eva, and the earth is family. Each join undone opened a teaching. And each one still sounds whole when it's joined again.

how: Vedic reciters learn a hymn from a teacher by ear, both as the joined samhita and as the word-by-word padapatha, and some go on to patterned recitations; families teach children shlokas the same way, by repeating after an elder.

games.q: a friend says, 'why memorize Sanskrit verses when they're all online?' what does the Hindu tradition of shruti say?
o: the Veda is heard: kept alive by being learned by ear and said aloud, teacher to student.
she's right; once it's written down, nobody needs to say it.
only priests are allowed to know the words.
games.why: shruti means what is heard. the Vedas were kept by ear for thousands of years, joined and unjoined, and families still teach shlokas by repeating after an elder.

practice: Do it the way Hindu children still learn a shloka, repeating after an elder. Say namaste whole. Then the padapatha way: namah, a pause, te.

Then whole again. Do the same with vasudhaiva kutumbakam: vasudha, eva, kutumbakam, then joined. Then let the words go, and let the breath do the same: a small pause at the end of each out-breath, and the next breath joining on.

wordCard.voice: Sandhi plainly: the joins between words, made by the mouth, and undone, word by word, in the padapatha, so the Veda could be kept by heart.

orig.note: Sanskrit: śruti, what is heard; the Vedas, received by the seers and passed on by ear.

carryVoice: The week's line: shruti, the Veda is heard, and kept by heart. The partridges remember. Another week, walked.
